title: 1 Foundations of Narrative Distance
use_cases: Use when determining the level of intimacy and emotional access the reader has to a character
Configure when deciding between internal and external focalization for specific plot points
Implement when selecting a narrative perspective to control the flow of information and suspense
Use when distinguishing between the stylistic tone of a voice and its physical distance from the events
content:
Definition

> The gap between the narrator’s viewpoint and the events or characters being described. It determines whether the reader feels like a confidant or an observer.

Purpose

- Shapes reader experience by setting intimacy level.
- Controls information flow—what is revealed, what remains hidden.
- Influences emotional engagement and suspense.

| Type | Characteristics | Typical Uses | Close (Intimate) | Narrator shares thoughts, feelings, sensory details; often first‑person or close third‑person. | Personal diaries, introspective novels, character‑driven stories. | Distant (Detached) | Narrator observes events without internal commentary; often omniscient or limited third‑person. | Historical epics, broad social dramas, objective reportage. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

I narrator: immediate access to inner life; limited to what the narrator knows. Variants include first‑person plural and a distinct narrator voice.

> Example: In “ The Catcher in the Rye,” Holden’s voice is unmistakably first‑person, giving readers direct insight into his thoughts.

You narrator: rare, creates direct address. Can be immersive or instructive.

> Example: The novel“If on a winter’s night you could see the world” uses second person to pull readers into the protagonist’s experience.

He/She/They narrator: subdivided into limited and omniscient.

- Limited Third‑Person – follows one character; close to that character’s thoughts.
- Omniscient Third‑Person – all‑knowing, can jump between characters and scenes.

Definition

> The focus of the narrative: the perspective through which events are filtered.

Types

- Internal Focalization – narrator’s own thoughts/feelings.
- External Focalization – narrator observes others’ actions without internal commentary.

The voice is the tone, style, personality of the narrator; the distance is how far that voice is from the story’s events. A sarcastic voice can still be close or distant depending on focalization.
